title: Symplex: Improved Pairing-Based zkSNARK using Partial Fraction Techniques
authors: Charanjit S. Jutla and Arnab Roy
abstract:
We present Symplex, a pairing-based zkSNARK for R1CS that preserves the syntax of Groth16: a $2G_1{+}1G_2$ proof, and a verifier with three pairings and one public-input multi-scalar multiplication (MSM), while {\it strictly reducing prover cost}. For constraint count $n$, wire count $m$, public-input count $\ell$, and $\kappa=\min\{n,m+1\}$, Symplex's prover uses four FFTs of size $n$ rather than the six of our coset-Lagrange Groth16 comparator, and its larger $G_1$-MSM has width $m+n-\ell+4$ rather than the adaptively based Groth16 width
$2\kappa+m+n-\ell+3$.

The matched Groth16 prover derives three length-$n$ vectors from the R1CS instance, converts each between coefficient and evaluation form, and commits the quotient with a size-$n$ coset-Lagrange column, resulting in six FFTs in total.  Its usual monomial quotient column has one fewer CRS element but requires a final inverse FFT.

Symplex instead uses the partial-fraction techniques of Jutla, Nema, Roy (EuroCrypt 2026) allowing the output-wire selector polynomials to be precomputed into the per-wire CRS bundles during setup. So, only the left- and right-wire vectors require FFT-based processing at proving time. The verifier is unchanged (three pairings, one public-input MSM). On a BLS12-381 prototype of Symplex that shares sparse R1CS, FFT, and pairing code with Groth16, a Circom circuit chaining SHA-256 ten times
gives a $1.84\times$ prover speedup with online verification at $\approx 2.6\,\mathrm{ms}$ for both schemes. The uniform algebraic extraction argument, perfect completeness, and perfect zero-knowledge are machine-checked in Lean~4.

Polymath (Lipmaa, CRYPTO 2024) and PARI (Dellepere, Mishra, and Shirzad, USENIX Security 2026) shrink the proof using a squared R1CS arithmetization. Polymath proves soundness in the AGMOS model, and PARI does not provide zero-knowledge in the stated construction. Symplex keeps Groth16's proof shape and standard R1CS arithmetization, and is proved knowledge-sound in the standard  Generic Group Model.

1   Introduction

Zero-knowledge succinct non-interactive arguments of knowledge (zkSNARKs)
[Mic00, GGPR13, PHGR13, Gro16] over pairing-friendly groups are a standard
tool in practical cryptography. Among them, Groth16 [Gro16] remains the stan-
dard proof system for rank-one constraint systems (R1CS), the arithmetization
derived from the quadratic arithmetic programs (QAPs) of [GGPR13], with
circuit-specific trusted setup. Its proof is three group elements (2 G1 +1 G2 ), its
online verifier consists of three pairings and one public-input multi-scalar mul-
tiplication (MSM), and it offers perfect zero-knowledge. Groth16 has anchored
production deployments for nearly a decade, from the shielded payments of Zcash
Sapling [HBHW24] and Loopring’s zk-rollup [DWF+ 20] to zkLogin blockchain
authentication [BCJ+ 24]. Other approaches to zkSNARKS which can be trans-
parent and post-quantum-friendly are based on interactive oracle proofs [BCS16]
and STARKs [BBHR18]. These offer setup-freeness but at the cost of larger
proofs and longer verification time. Our work is in the pairing-friendly group
setting.
    The prover in Groth16, however, pays for its minimal verifier. The Groth16
prover in arkworks [ark22] and snarkjs [ide24] performs three forward and three
inverse size-n FFTs to evaluate the critical QAP quotient h(X) of [GGPR13,
Gro16], followed by a final inverse FFT for its usual monomial t(x)/δ column.
More specifically, it switches the three wire-indexed evaluations ua, va, wa
between coefficient and evaluation form, and assembles a G1 -MSM of width 3m+
(n − ℓ) + 4 using Pippenger’s algorithm [Pip80]. For the matched comparison in
this paper, we give Groth16 a size-n coset-Lagrange t(x)/δ column: this adds one
G1 basis element, makes the corresponding width 3m+(n−ℓ)+5, and removes the
final inverse FFT, leaving six FFTs total [CJL+ 26]. These costs motivate several
recent lines of work, but their objectives and arithmetizations differ. Section 2
gives a dedicated account of the partial-fraction antecedent, short-proof systems
over squaring arithmetizations, and dynamic Groth16 variants. It also states the
parameter conventions needed to compare them without conflating unlike prover
costs.

Our contribution: Symplex. We present Symplex, 3 a pairing-based zkSNARK for
R1CS that matches Groth16 on proof structure (2 G1 +1 G2 ), arithmetization,
perfect zero-knowledge, and verifier cost (three online pairings and one public-
input MSM, without any field-element opening and without any public-input
interpolation), while reducing prover cost. Symplex’s prover performs four FFTs
of size n instead of the matched Groth16 comparator’s six (Section 6.2) and
a G1 -MSM of width n + (m − ℓ) + 4 in place of Groth16’s adaptively based
width 2κ + m + (n − ℓ) + 3, where κ = min{n, m + 1} (Table 2). Knowledge-
soundness is proved in the standard GGM [Sho97] (Section 7.3), without relying
on AGMOS and, like Groth16, without random oracle or Fiat–Shamir transform.
The uniform algebraic extraction argument, perfect completeness, and perfect
honest-verifier zero-knowledge have additionally been machine-checked in Lean 4
(Section 9).

This section outlines Symplex informally. We recall the partial-fraction primitives

construction. Partial fractions avoid the switching between coefficient and evalu-

in the basis {1/(X − α)}α the pairing-friendly product law is already point-wise

3.6    Why point-wise products are native to partial fractions

operations are conjugate via the DFT, and any protocol that wants to express
a Hadamard relation as a polynomial identity in the monomial basis must con-

(Remark 2).

This section outlines notation and recalls the cryptographic background used in

4.1   Notation and bilinear groups
We work over a finite field Fp of prime order p with log p = poly(λ). A bilinear
group system is a tuple (Fp , G1 , G2 , GT , e, g, h) of three cyclic groups of order
p together with a non-degenerate bilinear pairing e : G1 × G2 → GT , where
g generates G1 and h generates G2 . We use the bracket [EHK+ 13] notation
[x]1 := g x ∈ G1 , [y]2 := hy ∈ G2 , and [z]T := e(g, h)z ∈ GT , so that pairing
equations take the multiplicative form [x]1 · [y]2 = [xy]T .

4.2   Non-interactive zero-knowledge arguments of knowledge
Throughout, Symplex is presented as a quadruple (Setup, Prove, Verify, Sim) for a
relation R encoded by an R1CS instance: the CRS σ is output at setup, honest
proofs are arguments π accepted by Verify, and Sim establishes perfect zero-
knowledge. We prove perfect completeness and perfect zero-knowledge in Sec-
tion 7, and computational knowledge soundness in the generic group model (Sec-
tion 7.3). The formal syntax of non-interactive arguments and the definitions of
completeness, zero-knowledge, knowledge soundness, and preprocessing SNARK
succinctness are recalled in Appendix A.

4.3   The generic group model
We use the generic group model (GGM) of Shoup [Sho97], extended with a
bilinear-pairing oracle. For each s ∈ {1, 2, T }, the experiment samples an inde-
pendent random injective encoding encs : Fp → {0, 1}κ , where 2κ ≥ p. The
adversary receives only the encodings of the public group elements and accesses
the groups through oracles that, on valid handles, compute
                 encs (a), encs (b) ↦−→ encs (ca + c′ b)   (c, c′ ∈ Fp ),
                 enc1 (a), enc2 (b) ↦−→ encT (ab).
The first oracle implements group operations and scalar multiplication in Gs ,
while the second implements the pairing. Equality is equality of handles, and


                                          11
malformed handles are rejected. In the symmetric setting G1 = G2 , a single
source-group encoding is used and the pairing oracle accepts two source-group
handles.
    Thus a generic adversary can manipulate group elements and test relations
among them, but cannot inspect their representations or otherwise access their
discrete logarithms. Moreover, every source-group handle in an oracle transcript
has a coefficient vector expressing its exponent as an Fp -linear combination of the
source-group inputs. The GGM simulator can recover these vectors by tracking
the oracle calls. These are the symbolic representations used by the knowledge
extractor in Section 7.3. Distinct formal expressions can be assigned the same
handle only when their evaluations collide, whose probability is bounded by the
standard Schwartz–Zippel and union-bound argument.

Completeness and zero-knowledge. For completeness, Lean verifies the partial-
fraction recombination formula for Hlin and establishes the honest verification
identity by comparing its four nonzero graded components, corresponding to
the monomials yz, y, z, and 1. The evaluated completeness theorem is proved
directly in the field. Perfect HVZK is formalized as equality of probability mass
functions: the map from the honest coins (r, s) to (A, B) is constructed as an
explicit affine bijection of F2p , and the simulator’s value of C is identified with
the honest value using completeness. Thus the distributional claim is exact and
does not rely on an informal conditioning argument.

Knowledge-soundness. The soundness proof mechanizes the coefficient argument
of Lemma 3. Lean proves a single theorem for arbitrary R1CS matrices by com-
paring a fixed set of coefficients in the formal verification identity. These coeffi-
cients are indexed jointly by monomials in Y, Z, Γ, ∆ and by partial-fraction pole
coordinates. The resulting coefficient equations first imply az by = 1 and bγ = 0,
then show that the coefficients of the private-wire CRS elements occurring in
A lie in the simultaneous kernel of L, R, O, and finally recover the L-, R-, and
O-row relations from the coefficients of Y pα , Zpα , and p2α . The result is one
extractor theorem quantified over arbitrary fields and arbitrary R1CS matrices.
Although az by = 1 permits the conventional normalization az = by = 1 by in-
versely rescaling A and B, the Lean proof retains the original proof elements
and uses the relation az by = 1 directly. Its extracted private-wire vector initially
contains a correction formed from the δ-coefficient of B and the private-wire
coefficients of A. Lean proves that this correction lies in the simultaneous kernel
of L, R, and O, so removing it does not change any constraint. This gives the
simpler extractor from the coefficients of C used in Theorem 4.

Validation and axiomatic dependencies. The partial-fraction structure constants
are checked internally by evaluation lemmas and externally against an indepen-

proofs, extraction, malformed witnesses, degenerate instances, and the known
single-trapdoor forgery. Definitional-equality checks ensure that the top-level se-

Scope. The mechanized soundness theorem starts from an algebraic strategy
that satisfies the verification equation as a formal identity. It does not formalize
the reduction from a Type-III generic-group adversary to those source-group co-

at the sampled setup values to formal acceptance. These are the probabilis-

pairing equation, and the circuit-to-R1CS reduction, are likewise outside the
Lean development. Consequently, the formalization checks the algebraic core on
which the paper’s security reductions rely while leaving those standard cryp-

C.4   AI-Assisted Discovery and Lean Verification

collection of coefficient identities. That reduction isolated the exact requirement
